No, you are wrong. You are mingling together different things (tax, a specific release clause tax and installments). Firstly, your use of the word "tax" makes it sound like it's a regular tax and it happens in every transfer. That's not the case. The tax you described in certain cases is very specific as it only affects breaking release clauses of players in certain leagues. Thus to make it easier to understand, I'll refer to that tax with a capital T (Tax).  Those release clauses are broken extremely rarely and that Tax is a big reason for it as the buying team practically has to pay extra money that benefit neither team really. So for example a certain player, his release clause is a certain amount. One club makes a offer to another club. If the other club accepts, One club pays only that amount including regular tax. If the other club is adamant not to sell and refuses, One club can go to the federation (or something like that), pay the amount cash plus the extra Tax to break the release clause and circumvent the other club and sign the player.  That's what also happened with other players. A certain club is notorious for not negotiating with buying clubs and forcing them to break release clauses which is inconvient and costly as it required the money to be paid instantly and not in installments plus the extra Tax. As far as reports go, you are correct that in the extremely low number of this kind of cases, the extra Tax is usually not added it in the reported cost. There have been a number of times though that I've seen the extra tax added in. All that though is irrelevant with a certain player's case and 99.99% of the transfers overall as in all of those transfers the regular tax is included in the reported transfer prices. In a certain player's leaked contract for example it said that the price is an amount plus 5% tax. Secondly, installments and extra clauses. The transfer prices are rarely disclosured officially and the paying method is practically never disclusured. In general though, if the media have the appropriate info, they will report the actual money paid. For example a player could have been bought for an amount but the club chose to pay three installments for a total sum of a higher amount, chances are the media will report the higher amount. That's what practically happens all the time since most of the transfers are paid in installments and not all up front. As for clauses it depends as there are "easy" clauses like for example a certain player's about a club qualifying to the Champions League and there are "hard" clauses like winning the CL or being a top 3 ballon d'or nominee etc. The easy clauses are usually either reported in the sum altogether or reported as an amount plus an extra and in the article it's said what the clauses are or how easy they are to be achieved. The harder clauses are more rarely disclosured initially and they usually become known after they've met, usually by the seller who leaks the info as a way to show they made a good deal in their sale. Real Madrid specifically has a very solid base on being owned by club members and its history which makes it hard for a sole person to run it to the ground. Experience is also an important factor and there are times where going for the older player is the right move. Examples of that are Ronaldo, Modric, Kroos who were already established players and helped the club immensely. For example, last summer Kante seemed available but the club didn't look at all willing to go for him. As for the media, I don't pay too much attention to it. If you are doing your job well, you'll eventually force even the biggest haters to recognize your value.
